questions.stem: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.explanation: Tokyo, 「とうきょう」 (toukyou), is the capital and largest city. Kyoto was the capital for over a thousand years before that, and Osaka is a major city to its west.

questions.stem: In which direction is Japan from Australia?
questions.explanation: Japan lies to the north of Australia in the western Pacific, off the east coast of mainland Asia. Because the two countries are roughly north and south of each other, their time zones are close.

questions.stem: How many main islands make up most of Japan?
questions.explanation: Japan has thousands of islands, but four main ones: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku. Most people live on Honshu.

questions.stem: Which is the largest of Japan's four main islands?
questions.explanation: Honshu is by far the largest, and Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka are all on it. Hokkaido is second in size and lies to the north.

questions.stem: Which of the four main islands lies furthest north?
questions.explanation: Hokkaido is the northern island, known for snowy winters and its snow festival in Sapporo. Kyushu is in the south-west and Shikoku is the smallest of the four.

questions.stem: What is Mt Fuji?
options: An island off the coast to the south of Tokyo
A famous temple in the old capital
questions.explanation: Mt Fuji, 3,776 metres high, is Japan's tallest mountain and a volcano on Honshu. On clear days it can be seen from Tokyo.

questions.stem: In 「ふじ山」 (fujisan), the Japanese name for Mt Fuji, what does 山 mean?
questions.explanation: 山 means mountain, and in mountain names it is read さん (san). It only sounds like the title さん used after people's names; the two are different words.

questions.stem: Into how many prefectures is Japan divided?
questions.explanation: Japan has 47 prefectures, the regions used for local government, a little like Australia's states but much smaller. Tokyo and Hokkaido are each one of them.

questions.stem: What does 「日本」 (nihon), the Japanese name for Japan, mean word for word?
questions.explanation: 日 is sun and 本 is origin. Seen from China, Japan lay towards the sunrise, which is why it is called the Land of the Rising Sun.

questions.stem: What is on the Japanese flag?
options: A red sun with rays on a blue background
A red circle on a white background
A white circle on a red background
A red cross on a white background
questions.explanation: The flag is a red disc, the sun, on white. Its Japanese name 「ひのまる」 (hinomaru) means 'circle of the sun'.

questions.stem: What is the currency of Japan?
questions.explanation: The yen is written 円 and said えん (en) in Japanese. The won is Korea's currency and the yuan is China's.

questions.stem: When it is summer in Australia, what season is it in Japan?
questions.explanation: Japan is in the northern hemisphere, so its seasons are the opposite of Australia's. Christmas falls in winter there, and the school year begins in spring.

questions.stem: Which city was Japan's capital for over a thousand years before Tokyo?
questions.explanation: Kyoto, 「きょうと」 (kyouto), was the imperial capital from the late 700s until the 1860s. It is still famous for its temples, shrines and gardens.

questions.stem: Which three scripts are used together in everyday Japanese writing?
questions.explanation: A single sentence can use all three: 「わたしはケーキを食べます。」 (watashi wa keeki o tabemasu.) has hiragana, katakana for 'cake' and the kanji 食. Hangul is Korean and pinyin is a way of writing Chinese sounds.

questions.stem: Where did kanji originally come from?
questions.explanation: Kanji are Chinese characters, brought to Japan more than 1,500 years ago. The word 「かんじ」 (kanji) itself means 'Chinese characters'.

questions.stem: How did hiragana develop?
options: From simplified, flowing forms of whole kanji
From a single small part taken from each kanji
From the letters of the Latin alphabet
From the letters of the Korean alphabet
questions.explanation: Hiragana grew out of kanji written quickly in a cursive style, which is why they look rounded. Katakana are the ones made from parts of kanji.

questions.stem: How did katakana develop?
options: From marks used to write music
From small parts taken from kanji
From simplified, flowing forms of whole kanji
From the letters of the Latin alphabet
questions.explanation: Katakana were made by taking one piece of a kanji, which is why they look angular. Hiragana come from whole kanji written in a flowing style.

questions.stem: Which script is mainly used for words borrowed from other languages?
questions.explanation: Borrowed words such as 「テレビ」 (terebi, television) and 「ピザ」 (piza, pizza) are written in katakana, as are most foreign names.

questions.stem: Which script is used for particles such as は and を and for verb endings?
questions.explanation: Hiragana carry the grammar: particles, and the endings in words like 「食べます」 (tabemasu), where the kanji 食 gives the meaning and べます the ending.

questions.stem: What does a single kanji usually stand for?
options: A tone of voice to use when speaking
A meaning, as well as one or more sounds
One sound only, like a letter of the alphabet
questions.explanation: 山 means 'mountain' and can be read やま (yama) or さん (san). Hiragana and katakana, by contrast, stand for sounds only.

questions.stem: Roughly how many kanji are on Japan's official list for everyday use?
questions.explanation: The list of kanji for general use has just over 2,000 characters, and students learn about half of them in primary school. Many more kanji exist, but they are rare.

questions.stem: How many basic hiragana are there?
questions.explanation: There are 46 basic hiragana, and katakana has a matching set of 46. Two small marks turn some of them into extra sounds, such as か (ka) into が (ga).

questions.stem: What is romaji?
options: A style of handwriting for kanji
The script used for borrowed words
An older form of the Japanese language
Japanese written in the Latin alphabet
questions.explanation: Romaji spells Japanese sounds in the alphabet English uses, as in 'sushi' or 'arigatou'. It helps learners and appears on signs, but Japanese is not normally written in it.

questions.stem: In which directions can Japanese be written?
options: Across from left to right, or down in columns
Only across the page from right to left, never down
Only down the page in columns
Only across from left to right
questions.explanation: Textbooks and websites usually run left to right like English. Novels, newspapers and manga often use vertical columns that are read from top to bottom, starting on the right.

questions.stem: A Japanese book printed in vertical columns opens from which side?
options: Either side, as the reader chooses
What an English reader would call the back
The same side as an English book
The bottom edge, like a calendar
questions.explanation: Vertical columns are read from right to left, so the spine is on the right and the first page is where an English book would end. Manga open the same way.

questions.stem: Japanese has no capital letters. How can a reader spot foreign names and borrowed words?
options: They are usually written in katakana
They are printed in a larger size
They are always written in hiragana instead
questions.explanation: Katakana does part of the job capital letters and italics do in English: 「オーストラリア」 (oosutoraria) stands out at once in a line of hiragana and kanji.

questions.stem: Why is Japanese written with kanji when every word could be spelt in hiragana?
options: Kanji show meaning and tell apart words that sound the same
Hiragana cannot be used to write verbs
Kanji are needed to write borrowed words
Hiragana are only ever used by young children
questions.explanation: Japanese has many words that sound alike, and kanji make them clear on the page. Kanji also help the reader see where words begin, since Japanese has no spaces.

questions.stem: In the name 「やまだはなこ」 (yamada hanako), which part is the family name?
options: Neither part, as it is left out
It changes with the person's age
questions.explanation: Japanese puts the family name first and the given name second, the reverse of English. Hanako Yamada in English order is 「やまだはなこ」 in Japanese.

questions.stem: Your teacher is Ms Yamada. How would Japanese students usually address her?
questions.explanation: Teachers are addressed with 先生 (sensei), on its own or after the family name. Students would not call a teacher by a given name.

questions.stem: When should you never use さん (san)?
questions.explanation: さん shows respect for someone else, so adding it to your own name sounds as if you are praising yourself. In a self-introduction you just say 「わたしはサムです。」 (watashi wa samu desu.)

questions.stem: Which title is commonly used after boys' names, for example by classmates and teachers?
questions.explanation: くん is used mostly for boys and young men by friends, teachers and seniors. さま is a very respectful title for customers, and 先生 is for teachers and doctors.

questions.stem: Which title sounds affectionate and is used for small children and close friends?
questions.explanation: ちゃん is a friendly, affectionate version of さん, used for little children, family and close friends. Using it with a teacher would be far too familiar.

questions.stem: Why do Japanese speakers often avoid 「あなた」 (anata, 'you') when being polite?
options: 「あなた」 is used in writing and never in speech
Using the person's name with さん sounds more respectful
「あなた」 is a rude word that should never be said
「あなた」 only means 'you' when talking to a group
questions.explanation: Saying 「たなかさんは」 (tanaka-san wa) to Tanaka-san herself is the polite way to say 'you'. 「あなた」 is not rude in itself, but it can sound distant or too direct, so it is used much less than English 'you'.

questions.stem: Which word should you use for your own mother when talking to a teacher?
questions.explanation: Japanese uses plain words for your own family when talking to outsiders and respectful words for other people's. So it is 「母」 (haha) to a teacher, but 「お母さん」 (okaasan) for the teacher's mother or a friend's.

questions.stem: What do the prefixes お and ご, as in 「おちゃ」 (ocha) and 「ごはん」 (gohan), add to a word?
questions.explanation: お and ご make a word sound polite or respectful: 「おなまえは何ですか。」 (onamae wa nan desu ka.) asks someone's name politely. Some words, like 「ごはん」, are almost always said with the prefix.

questions.stem: What is おじぎ (ojigi)?
questions.explanation: Bowing is the usual way to greet, thank, apologise and say goodbye in Japan. People still shake hands with visitors from overseas, sometimes with a small bow as well.

questions.stem: What does a deeper, longer bow usually show?
options: That the person is in a hurry
That the two people are already close friends
More respect or a more serious apology
questions.explanation: The deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it shows. Friends give a quick nod, while a formal apology can involve a long, low bow.

questions.stem: Which greeting is used in the morning?
options: おはようございます (ohayou gozaimasu)
questions.explanation: 「おはようございます」 is 'good morning'; with friends it shortens to 「おはよう」. 「こんにちは」 is for the daytime, 「こんばんは」 for the evening and 「おやすみなさい」 for going to bed.

questions.stem: What do people say as they leave home in the morning?
questions.explanation: 「いってきます」 means roughly 'I'm off, and I'll be back'. The family answers 「いってらっしゃい」 (itterasshai), 'go and come back'.

questions.stem: What do people say when they arrive back home?
questions.explanation: 「ただいま」 means 'I'm home'. It is part of a pair of set phrases with no exact English match, said every day in most homes.

questions.stem: Someone comes home and says 「ただいま」 (tadaima). What does the family reply?
questions.explanation: 「おかえりなさい」 means 'welcome home'. 「いってらっしゃい」 is the reply to 「いってきます」, said when someone is leaving.

questions.stem: Which phrase can mean both 'excuse me' and 'sorry'?
questions.explanation: 「すみません」 gets a waiter's attention, apologises for a small mistake and can even thank someone for trouble they have taken. 「どうぞ」 means 'please, go ahead'.

questions.stem: When is 「はじめまして」 (hajimemashite) used?
options: When saying goodbye at the end of the school day
When meeting someone for the first time
When leaving for a long holiday
Before starting to eat a meal
questions.explanation: 「はじめまして」 opens a first meeting, and a self-introduction often ends with 「どうぞよろしく」 (douzo yoroshiku), 'nice to meet you'.

questions.stem: In which month does the Japanese school year begin?
questions.explanation: The school year starts in April, when cherry trees are often in flower, and ends in March. Australian schools start in late January or early February.

questions.stem: What happens during そうじ (souji) time at a Japanese school?
options: Students eat a snack in the playground
Students practise for the sports carnival
Students sit a short quiz on the day's work
Students clean their classrooms and school
questions.explanation: In most schools students clean classrooms, corridors and toilets themselves every day. It is seen as part of learning responsibility.

questions.stem: What are ぶかつ (bukatsu) at a Japanese school?
options: The uniforms students wear on formal occasions
The tests students sit at the end of each term
The lunches students bring from home in a small wooden box
Clubs such as sport, music or art, held after classes
questions.explanation: Club activities are a big part of school life, and many students attend most days after school and sometimes at weekends.

questions.stem: What is きゅうしょく (kyuushoku) at a Japanese school?
options: A trip that students take together at the end of the school year
A break for students to clean the playground
School lunch, often served by students in the classroom
The morning assembly held in the school hall
questions.explanation: In primary and many junior high schools, lunch is provided by the school. Students take turns to serve it, and the class eats together in the room.

questions.stem: What do students usually do at the entrance to a Japanese school building?
options: Show a pass to a guard
questions.explanation: Just as at home, outdoor shoes stay at the entrance. Students keep them in shoe lockers and wear indoor shoes called 「うわばき」 (uwabaki) inside.

questions.stem: How is Japanese schooling usually divided?
options: Seven years of primary, three of junior high, two of senior high
Five years of primary, four of junior high, three of senior high
Six years of primary, then six years of one secondary school
Six years of primary, three of junior high, three of senior high
questions.explanation: The usual pattern is 6–3–3. Primary and junior high school, nine years in all, are compulsory.

questions.stem: Which stages of school are compulsory in Japan?
options: All twelve years of primary and high school
questions.explanation: Compulsory schooling is the six years of primary and three of junior high. Almost all students continue to senior high school anyway.

questions.stem: An Australian Year 8 student is about the same age as a Japanese student in which year?
options: The second year of junior high school
The eighth year of primary school
The first year of senior high school
The third year of senior high school
questions.explanation: Japanese primary school is six years, so Year 8 matches 「中学二年生」 (chuugaku ninensei), the second year of junior high. There is no eighth year of primary school.

questions.stem: What do people say before they start eating?
options: ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita)
questions.explanation: 「いただきます」 means 'I humbly receive'. It thanks everyone and everything that made the meal possible, and is said with hands together.

questions.stem: What do people say when they have finished eating?
options: ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita)
questions.explanation: 「ごちそうさまでした」 thanks the cook and the host for the meal. Among family and friends it is often shortened to 「ごちそうさま」.

questions.stem: Which habit with chopsticks is considered bad manners?
options: Saying いただきます before picking them up
Standing them upright in a bowl of rice
Resting them on a small chopstick rest
Lifting the rice bowl closer to your mouth
questions.explanation: Chopsticks stood upright in rice recall an offering made at funerals, so it is avoided at the table. Resting them on a holder is good manners.

questions.stem: Why do people avoid passing food from one pair of chopsticks to another?
options: It is the way to pay at a restaurant
It is done only at New Year
It recalls a custom at funerals
Chopsticks are meant only for the cook
questions.explanation: At a Japanese funeral, family members pass the bones from one pair of chopsticks to another. Doing it with food reminds people of that, so food is put on a plate instead.

questions.stem: How is slurping noodles such as ramen seen in Japan?
options: It is always considered very rude
It is allowed only for small children
It is allowed at home but never in a shop
It is normal and not considered rude
questions.explanation: Slurping noodles is common and can show that you are enjoying them. It also cools hot noodles on the way in.

questions.stem: What is a べんとう (bentou)?
options: A packed meal in a box
questions.explanation: A bentou is a boxed meal, often rice with small portions of other foods. Students may take one to school, and shops and train stations sell them.

questions.stem: Apart from the topping, what is the main ingredient of sushi?
questions.explanation: The word sushi refers to the vinegared rice. Raw fish is a common topping, but sushi can also be made with egg, vegetables or cooked seafood.

questions.stem: How is lifting a rice bowl up close to your mouth seen at a Japanese meal?
options: It is only allowed at New Year
It is only done with soup
questions.explanation: Small bowls of rice and soup are held up while eating, which makes chopsticks easier to use. Leaning down to a bowl left on the table is what looks careless.

questions.stem: What is the げんかん (genkan) in a Japanese home?
options: The entrance area where shoes are taken off
The main room where visiting guests are entertained
The small garden at the back of the house
The room where the family takes a bath
questions.explanation: The げんかん is a little lower than the rest of the floor. Shoes come off there, and you step up into the house in socks or slippers.

questions.stem: What are たたみ (tatami)?
options: Cushions for sitting on the floor
Thick floor mats of woven straw
questions.explanation: Tatami cover the floor of traditional rooms. Even slippers come off before you walk on them. The sliding paper doors are 「しょうじ」 (shouji).

questions.stem: How is the size of a traditional Japanese room often described?
options: By how many doors lead into it
By how many tatami mats cover its floor
By how many windows it has
By how many people sleep in it
questions.explanation: Tatami come in a standard size, so a room is described as six mats or eight mats. The habit is still used for rooms with other flooring.

questions.stem: What is a ふとん (futon) in a Japanese home?
options: A sliding door that divides two rooms
A wooden tub used for taking a bath
Bedding laid on the floor at night and put away by day
A low table with a heater fitted underneath it
questions.explanation: A traditional futon is a mattress and quilt spread on the tatami at night and folded into a cupboard in the morning, so the room can be used by day.

questions.stem: In a Japanese bath, what do you do before getting into the tub?
options: Pour some soap into the bathwater
Wash and rinse yourself outside the tub
Get into the tub and wash with soap there
Let the water out and fill it again
questions.explanation: The bathtub is for soaking, not washing, and the same hot water is often shared by the family. So everyone washes and rinses first, outside the tub.

questions.stem: When is おしょうがつ (oshougatsu)?
options: The start of the school year in April
The hottest part of summer in August
The cherry blossom season in spring
New Year, at the start of January
questions.explanation: おしょうがつ, New Year, is the most important holiday of the year. Families gather, eat special food and visit a shrine or temple.

questions.stem: What is おとしだま (otoshidama)?
options: A special soup eaten at New Year
A greeting card sent to friends at New Year
A dance performed at New Year
Money given to children at New Year
questions.explanation: Children receive おとしだま from parents and relatives, usually in small decorated envelopes. New Year cards are 「ねんがじょう」 (nengajou).

questions.stem: What is はつもうで (hatsumoude)?
options: The first meal eaten on New Year's morning
The first snow of the winter season
The first visit to a shrine or temple in the new year
The first day back at school after the holidays
questions.explanation: Over the first days of January, crowds visit shrines and temples to pray for a good year ahead.

questions.stem: What do families do at ひなまつり (hinamatsuri) on 3 March?
options: Hang wishes on bamboo for two stars to read
Light paper lanterns to welcome the spirits of their ancestors
Display dolls and wish for girls' health and happiness
Fly carp streamers and wish for boys' strength
questions.explanation: ひなまつり is the Doll Festival, also called Girls' Day. Families with daughters set out a display of dolls in old court costume.

questions.stem: Which day, on 5 May, is celebrated with carp streamers called こいのぼり (koinobori)?
questions.explanation: 「こどもの日」 is Children's Day, a public holiday. Families fly carp streamers outside, wishing their children health and strength.

questions.stem: Why is the carp the symbol of こどもの日 (kodomo no hi)?
options: It lives for exactly one year, like a school class
It is said to swim up waterfalls, a sign of strength
It is said to be the only fish that lives in Japan's rivers
It is the food always eaten on that day
questions.explanation: An old story tells of a carp that swam up a waterfall and became a dragon. The carp stands for courage and success in the face of difficulty.

questions.stem: What do people do at たなばた (tanabata), usually on 7 July?
options: Set out dolls in old court costumes on a stand of red steps
Throw roasted beans to chase away bad luck
Give money to children in decorated envelopes
Write wishes on paper strips and hang them on bamboo
questions.explanation: Wishes are written on strips of coloured paper called 「たんざく」 (tanzaku) and tied to bamboo branches. Some areas hold たなばた in August instead.

questions.stem: The たなばた (tanabata) story tells of two stars who may meet only once a year. What keeps them apart?
options: The Milky Way, a river of stars
questions.explanation: The weaver princess and the cowherd, the stars Vega and Altair, are separated by the Milky Way. On the seventh night of the seventh month they are allowed to meet.

questions.stem: What is おぼん (obon)?
options: A winter holiday when children receive presents from family
A spring outing to look at cherry blossoms
A New Year visit to a shrine to pray
A summer festival honouring the spirits of ancestors
questions.explanation: During おぼん, in mid-August in most areas, many families return to their home towns, visit family graves and join in bon dances.

questions.stem: What is はなみ (hanami)?
options: A dance performed at summer festivals
Viewing cherry blossoms, often with a picnic
A meal of raw fish served on a long wooden board
A New Year card sent to friends and family
questions.explanation: はな means flower and み comes from 'look'. In spring, friends, families and workmates gather under the cherry trees to eat and enjoy the blossoms.

questions.stem: What is Golden Week in Japan?
options: The final week of the school year in March
A week of summer festivals in mid-August
Several public holidays together, from late April to early May
A week of big sales held in department stores just before New Year
questions.explanation: Golden Week strings together several public holidays, including こどもの日 (kodomo no hi) on 5 May. It is one of the busiest times of year for travel.

questions.stem: How common is Japanese as a subject in Australian schools?
options: It is not taught in Australian schools
It is taught only at university
It is compulsory in every state
It is one of the most widely studied languages
questions.explanation: Japanese has long been one of the most popular languages in Australian schools, alongside languages such as French, Italian, Chinese and Indonesian.

questions.stem: What is a sister-school link between an Australian and a Japanese school?
options: Two schools run by the same principal
A partnership for exchanges, visits and letters
Two schools that share a single building
A girls' school paired with a boys' school
questions.explanation: Many Australian schools have a sister school in Japan. Students write to each other, host visiting groups and sometimes go on exchange.

questions.stem: Which Japanese city is Melbourne's sister city?
questions.explanation: Melbourne and Osaka have been sister cities since 1978. Sydney's sister city in Japan is Nagoya, and Brisbane's is Kobe.

questions.stem: Which English word comes from Japanese?
questions.explanation: Karaoke is Japanese. Pizza is Italian, yoghurt comes from Turkish and chocolate from a language of Mexico by way of Spanish.

questions.stem: The English word 'emoji' comes from Japanese. What do its parts mean?
questions.explanation: 「え」 (e) means picture and 「もじ」 (moji) means written character. It only looks related to 'emotion'; the likeness is a coincidence.

questions.stem: What does 'tsunami' mean, word for word, in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 「つ」 (tsu) is harbour and 「なみ」 (nami) is wave. The name points to the damage the wave does when it reaches the coast and its harbours.

questions.stem: 'Karaoke' joins から (kara), 'empty', to a shortened form of which word?
questions.explanation: オケ (oke) is short for 「オーケストラ」 (ookesutora), orchestra. Karaoke is music with an 'empty orchestra': the recorded band plays without its singer.

questions.stem: Which English word does 「テレビ」 (terebi) come from?
questions.explanation: Many borrowed words are shortened: television became テレビ, and 'convenience store' became 「コンビニ」 (konbini). The telephone is 「でんわ」 (denwa).

questions.stem: 「パン」 (pan), the word for bread, was borrowed from which language?
questions.explanation: Portuguese traders reached Japan in the 1500s and brought bread, which they called pão. It is one of the oldest Western loanwords in Japanese.

questions.stem: Why do borrowed words often sound different in Japanese from the English?
options: Japanese has more vowel sounds than English does
Japanese syllables mostly end in a vowel, so vowels are added
Japanese speakers change words on purpose to make them shorter
Borrowed words have to use kanji, which change the sounds
questions.explanation: 'Ice cream' becomes 「アイスクリーム」 (aisukuriimu), because Japanese cannot end a syllable on s or m. Each consonant gets a vowel after it.

questions.stem: Some words look English but were made in Japan. What does 「サラリーマン」 (sarariiman) mean?
options: an office worker on a salary
a sailor on a cargo ship
questions.explanation: 「サラリーマン」 is built from English 'salary' and 'man', but the combination was made in Japan. An English speaker would say 'office worker'.

questions.stem: What does 'origami' mean in Japanese?
questions.explanation: おり (ori) comes from 'fold' and かみ (kami) is paper; the k becomes g when the two words join to make 「おりがみ」.

questions.stem: How many basic vowel sounds does Japanese have?
questions.explanation: Japanese has five: a, i, u, e and o, in the order of the kana chart. English has many more, which is why English words change when they are borrowed.

questions.stem: Which is a feature of Japanese pronunciation, compared with English?
options: It has far more vowel sounds than English
Almost every syllable ends in a vowel or ん (n)
Many words end in clusters of consonants like -sts
Many words begin with three consonants in a row
questions.explanation: Japanese syllables are mostly a consonant plus a vowel, like ka, mi or to. English words such as 'texts' or 'strengths' have no equivalent.

questions.stem: Why does it matter whether a Japanese vowel is short or long?
options: It never matters; both are understood the same
It can change the meaning, as in おばさん and おばあさん
A long vowel always makes a word sound more polite
A long vowel always turns a word into a question
questions.explanation: 「おばさん」 (obasan) is aunt and 「おばあさん」 (obaasan) is grandmother. Holding the vowel for longer makes a different word, so long vowels must be heard and written.

questions.stem: In what order is a date written in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Dates go from the biggest unit to the smallest, 〜年〜月〜日, just as names put the family first and addresses start with the prefecture.

questions.stem: How does Japanese show politeness differently from English?
options: By saying every sentence more loudly and slowly
By putting the most important word first
Through verb forms like です and ます and special polite words
Only by adding a word meaning 'please' to the end of a request
questions.explanation: English adds 'please' or 'could you'. Japanese builds politeness into the grammar: 「食べます」 (tabemasu) is polite where 「たべる」 (taberu) is plain, and there are respectful words such as 「お母さん」 (okaasan).
